items.title: Nine Coins Heavy
items.question: You have nine identical coins and one is slightly heavier. Using a balance scale, what is the fewest weighings that guarantee finding it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2. Splitting into three groups of three lets each weighing cut the candidates to a third.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. A balance has three outcomes, so two weighings can distinguish among nine possibilities.
items.lessonContent:
A balance yields three outcomes per use.
Each weighing can shrink options to a third.
Think in powers of three.
Plan the split before weighing.
Share this: find how many questions a three-way choice needs to reach one item.

items.title: Twenty Seven Coins
items.question: Among twenty-seven coins, one is heavier. What is the minimum number of balance weighings needed to identify it for certain?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 3. Three weighings can separate twenty-seven possibilities because three cubed is twenty-seven.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Dividing the set into thirds each time matches the three outcomes of the balance.
items.lessonContent:
Capacity grows as three to the power of trials.
Three weighings handle up to twenty-seven.
Split into thirds at each step.
Match method to the tool's outcomes.
Share this: compute how many items two three-way tests can sort.

items.title: Three Coins Heavy
items.question: With three coins and one known to be heavier, how many balance weighings are needed at minimum?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 1. Weighing one against another settles it in a single comparison.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. If one side drops, that coin is heavier; if they balance, the third is the culprit.
items.lessonContent:
A single comparison can split three ways.
Balance, left-heavy, and right-heavy cover all cases.
Design the weighing to use every outcome.
Efficiency comes from full use of information.
Share this: design one test that distinguishes three possibilities.

items.title: Twelve Unknown Coins
items.question: Among twelve coins one is counterfeit and may be heavier or lighter. What is the fewest balance weighings that guarantee identifying it and its direction?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 3. Twelve coins times two possible directions gives twenty-four cases, just within the twenty-seven that three weighings reach.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Twelve coins with two possible directions give twenty-four cases, and three weighings handle up to twenty-seven.
items.lessonContent:
Count the cases before planning.
Unknown direction doubles the possibilities.
Keep within the tool's capacity.
Design each weighing to split the cases evenly.
Share this: count the possible answers before choosing a method.

items.title: Eight Coins Heavy
items.question: One of eight coins is heavier than the rest. How many balance weighings are required at minimum?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2. Two weighings cover up to nine cases, so eight fits comfortably.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Nine is the capacity of two weighings, so eight coins need no more than that.
items.lessonContent:
Find the smallest power of three above your count.
Two weighings handle nine cases.
Choose the method by capacity.
Avoid unnecessary comparisons.

items.title: Three Outcomes
items.question: How many distinct results can a single balance-scale weighing produce?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 3. The left side can drop, the right side can drop, or the two can balance.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. That third outcome is what makes a balance more informative than a simple yes-or-no test.
items.lessonContent:
A tool's outcomes set its power.
Three results per use beat two.
Design tests to exploit every outcome.
Capacity follows from branching.

items.title: Four Coins Heavy
items.question: Among four coins one is heavier. What is the fewest balance weighings to identify it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2. Two weighings handle nine cases, and four coins fit within that capacity.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. A single weighing covers only three cases, so four coins require the second round.
items.lessonContent:
Compare the case count with the capacity.
One weighing covers three items.
Add rounds as the count grows.

items.title: Six Coins Heavy
items.question: Six pearls look identical, though one is heavier. On a balance, what is the fewest weighings that always find it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2. Six sits between three and nine, so two weighings suffice.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Since two weighings cover nine cases, six coins are comfortably within reach.
items.lessonContent:
Locate your count between the powers of three.
Round up to the next capacity.
Two weighings cover up to nine.

items.title: Hundred Coins Heavy
items.question: A jar holds a hundred near-identical marbles, one denser than the rest. With a balance, what is the smallest number of comparisons that always isolates it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 5. Four weighings cover eighty-one, while five cover two hundred and forty-three.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. You need the smallest power of three that reaches one hundred, which is the fifth.
items.lessonContent:
Find the next power of three above the count.
Four weighings reach eighty-one.
Five reach two hundred and forty-three.
Round capacity upward.

items.title: Two Coins Heavy
items.question: You have two coins and know one is heavier. How many weighings settle it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 1. Placing one coin against the other shows which side is heavier.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. Comparing the two directly is the only weighing required.
items.lessonContent:
The simplest comparison is often enough.
Two items need one weighing.

items.title: Thirteen Coins Heavy
items.question: One of thirteen coins is heavier. What is the minimum number of balance weighings needed?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 3. Two weighings cover only nine, while three cover twenty-seven.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Thirteen exceeds the capacity of two weighings, so a third is required.
items.lessonContent:
Check whether the count exceeds a capacity.
Two weighings stop at nine.
Three reach twenty-seven.
Exceed the limit means another round.

items.title: Nine Coins Light
items.question: Among nine coins one is lighter. How many balance weighings are needed to find it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2. Whether the odd coin is heavy or light, the three-way split works the same way.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. The direction of the anomaly does not change the number of splits needed.
items.lessonContent:
Direction changes which side rises.
The method stays the same.
Three-way splits work either way.

items.title: Three Weighings Capacity
items.question: Using a balance and knowing the odd coin is heavier, how many coins can three weighings distinguish at most?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 27. Three balanced weighings branch into three cubed possibilities.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 27. Each weighing triples the number of distinguishable cases.
items.lessonContent:
Capacity multiplies by three each round.
Three rounds give twenty-seven.
Plan the split to use all capacity.

items.title: Two Weighings Capacity
items.question: What is the largest set of coins a balance can fully sort in exactly two rounds, assuming one coin is known to be heavier?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 9. Two weighings branch three ways twice, giving nine cases.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 9. The capacity is the square of the number of outcomes per weighing.
items.lessonContent:
Each round multiplies the cases by three.
Two rounds give nine.
Exceeding capacity needs a third round.

items.title: Four Weighings Capacity
items.question: How many suspect coins can a balance resolve in four rounds if exactly one is heavier?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 81. Four rounds of three outcomes give three to the fourth power.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 81. Each extra weighing triples the previous capacity.
items.lessonContent:
Capacity grows by a factor of three.
Four rounds reach eighty-one.
Powers make scaling predictable.

items.title: One Weighing Capacity
items.question: At most how many coins can be told apart in a single use of a balance, given that one is heavier?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 3. One weighing gives three outcomes, so three coins can be told apart.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Balance, left-heavy, and right-heavy map to three distinct culprits.

items.question: Five brass buttons include one heavier copy. What is the least number of balance comparisons that guarantee locating it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2. Five exceeds the three covered by one weighing but sits within nine.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. One weighing cannot separate five candidates, but two can.

items.title: Pans on a Balance
items.question: How many pans does a balance scale use?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2. Two pans are compared against each other, plus the balanced case as a third outcome.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Two pans give three possible results: left down, right down, or level.
items.lessonContent:
Two pans compare two amounts at once.
The balanced case adds a third outcome.
The tool's design enables its method.

items.title: Seven Coins Heavy
items.question: A drawer holds seven similar stones, one heavier. What is the smallest number of weighings that always finds the odd stone?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2. Seven falls between three and nine, so two weighings cover it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. A single weighing covers only three coins, leaving four unresolved.

items.title: Ten Coins Heavy
items.question: Ten identical-looking tokens hide one heavier fake. How few balance weighings always expose it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 3. Ten exceeds nine, the reach of two weighings, so a third is needed.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Two weighings fall just short, which is why the count matters.

Just exceeding a capacity forces another round.

items.question: With a balance, how many coins can be checked at most in three weighings when the counterfeit may be heavier or lighter?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 12. Two directions per coin give twenty-four cases, just within the twenty-seven that three weighings reach.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 12. Unknown direction halves the capacity compared with a known direction.

items.question: Eight coins look the same except one, which is lighter. What is the smallest number of weighings that guarantees finding it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2. Eight is within the nine cases that two weighings can separate.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. The lighter direction is handled by the same three-way splitting.

The split works regardless of direction.

items.question: A chest of eighty-one coins contains one heavier specimen. What is the least number of weighings needed to be certain which?

items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Three weighings reach only twenty-seven, so four are required.

items.title: Two Weighings Unknown
items.question: With two balance weighings and an unknown heavier-or-lighter coin, how many coins can be handled at most?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 3. Nine outcomes lose some to the unknown direction, leaving three coins resolvable.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. The unknown doubles the cases, so two weighings cover far fewer coins than when direction is known.
items.lessonContent:

items.title: Twenty Four Coins
items.question: Twenty-four supposedly identical coins include one heavier fake. What is the minimum number of balance weighings to guarantee finding it?

items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Two weighings reach only nine, far short of twenty-four.
